opus-5.5.text:
I think accepting failure is almost a precondition for doing research at all. If you only work on things you're sure will succeed, you're probably not doing research. You're doing engineering on a problem someone else already solved.

For me, a lot of the projects people know about started as things that didn't quite work at first, or that many people thought weren't worth doing. When you build systems, especially open-source ones, you go through many versions. The first design is often wrong. You find out the abstraction doesn't fit, the performance isn't there, or nobody uses it. That's normal. The question is whether you can treat it as information rather than as a verdict on yourself.

Accepting failure also means being honest with yourself early. It's tempting to keep pushing an idea because you've invested so much in it. Sometimes the right thing is to say, okay, this direction isn't working, what did I learn, and what's the smaller thing inside it that actually holds up? Often that smaller piece becomes the foundation for the next thing.

There's an emotional side too. Paper rejections, experiments that don't pan out, a system you spent a year on that gets overtaken by something else. Those hurt, and I don't think you should pretend they don't. But over time I've come to see research as a long game. One failure is just one data point. If you keep working on problems you genuinely care about, and keep building and sharing things, the failures become part of the path rather than the end of it.

So I'd say accepting failure means giving yourself permission to try ambitious things. If you're afraid to fail, you'll naturally pick safer, smaller problems. And I think a lot of the most interesting work comes from being willing to be wrong for a while.

r001.rationale: The response urges pursuing problems one genuinely cares about and says accepting failure gives permission to try ambitious research.

r002.rationale: It describes research as iterative: designs fail, researchers learn, abandon or narrow a direction, and use what holds up as the foundation for the next effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, accepting failure isn't really a mindset I had to adopt — it's just the default condition of doing research. Most of what you try doesn't work. If I look back at XGBoost, or TVM, or MLC, the versions people know are maybe the fifth or tenth iteration. The earlier ones were slower, or the abstraction was wrong, or nobody wanted to use them. That's normal. The thing that matters is whether each failure tells you something.

So I try to think of failure as information. When an experiment doesn't work, the question isn't "was this a waste," it's "what did this rule out?" Sometimes a negative result narrows the design space more than a positive one would have. When I was working on the early compiler stack, we spent a long time on an approach to scheduling that we eventually threw away entirely. But going through that is what made it clear which parts of the problem were actually hard and which were just incidental. You can't skip that step by being smart; you have to pay for it.

The other side is being honest about the difference between a failed idea and a failed execution. Students often conclude an idea is bad when really the implementation had a bug, or the baseline was misconfigured. And the reverse happens too — people keep polishing something that fundamentally doesn't scale because they've already invested in it. So accepting failure also means being willing to cut your losses on something you like. That part is emotionally harder than the first part.

And I'd say, especially in systems and ML, you have to be comfortable with a long timescale. Sometimes an idea fails because the hardware or the ecosystem isn't there yet. Then two or three years later the same idea works. So I try not to treat a failure as a verdict on the idea forever — more like, this didn't work under these conditions, and I file it away. A lot of what looks like good intuition later is really just remembering what failed before and why.

r001.rationale: The response presents failure as a normal part of research and describes learning from failed attempts, iterating on projects, and cutting losses so work can continue.

r002.rationale: It mentions multiple iterations and abandoning one approach, but does not characterize research as repeatedly starting anew.

astra-6.text:
For me, accepting failure means being willing to learn that your idea was wrong. As a researcher, you start with something you don’t know how to do, so you can’t expect every attempt to work. You try something, look at the evidence, and ask, “What did this teach me? What should I change?”

That doesn’t mean you stop caring about the outcome. You still work hard to make the idea succeed. But you also have to separate yourself from the idea. An experiment failing doesn’t mean you’re a failure. Sometimes it gives you a clearer understanding of the problem, and that helps you take the next step.

r001.rationale: The response endorses working hard to make an idea succeed while accepting failed attempts, but it does not specify pursuing interesting research.

r002.rationale: It describes trying, learning from evidence, and changing course, but does not characterize research as repeatedly starting anew.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, accepting failure means being willing to find out that an idea doesn’t work, even when you’ve invested a lot of effort in it. As a researcher, you start with something you don’t know. If you only pursue things you’re certain will succeed, you limit what you can discover.

The important part is to learn from the failure. Was the assumption wrong? Was the experiment testing the right thing? Should we try a different approach, or move on? You can be persistent about a problem while being willing to let go of a particular solution. That’s the balance I try to keep.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should pursue uncertain ideas, persist with a problem, and accept that an idea may fail, conveying continued research despite failure.

r002.rationale: It describes starting with something unknown, but does not characterize research as repeatedly starting anew.
